value_domain: Count of employees paid under JobKeeper phase 1
value_source: ATO, Taxation statistics 2019-20, JobKeeper
variable_description: How many employees the business received a JobKeeper payment for during the original phase of the scheme. The ATO dates that phase as "JobKeeper phase 1 - 30 March to 27 September 2020", and every employee in it attracted the same flat rate of $1,500 a fortnight, so there is no tier split to go with the count as there is for the extension columns beside it. The figure comes from the entity's own monthly declarations rather than from payroll, so it is a claim count that the ATO paid on.
value_definition: A count of individuals, not full-time equivalents and not hours. It covers only the phase 1 window, so an employee claimed in both phases is counted here and again in jk2_emp_payment.
limitation: It is not the firm's workforce. Employees who failed the eligibility tests - short-tenure casuals, most temporary visa holders, and anyone nominated by another employer - are absent, so the count understates headcount by an amount that varies systematically with industry and with how casualised the firm is.
rationale: The ATO's taxation statistics page defines the JobKeeper phases and their dates, states that the statistics come from business monthly declarations, and separates the flat-rate original period from the tiered extension, which is what this column measures.
evidence_quote: JobKeeper phase 1 - 30 March to 27 September 2020
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The number of employees that received a JK v1 payment' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so it did not date the phase, name the flat rate, or say that eligibility rules shape the count.

value_domain: Count of employees paid under the JobKeeper extension
value_source: ATO, Taxation statistics 2019-20, JobKeeper
variable_description: How many employees the business received a JobKeeper payment for during the extension period of the scheme. The ATO splits that period into "JobKeeper extension 1 - 28 September 2020 to 3 January 2021" and "JobKeeper extension 2 - 4 January to 28 March 2021". Unlike phase 1 the extension paid two different rates, so this total should reconcile with jk2_emp_t1 and jk2_emp_t2 on the same row, and the ATO notes that the payment rate "changed in the JobKeeper extension and was split into 2 tiers".
value_definition: A count of individuals claimed across the extension as a whole, spanning both extension periods rather than either one. Individuals claimed in more than one period are not counted twice within this column.
limitation: A fall from jk1_emp_payment to this column mixes two very different things: employees who left or lost eligibility, and businesses that failed the actual decline in turnover test and dropped out of the scheme entirely. Without a turnover-test field the two cannot be separated, so this column should not be read as a job loss measure.
rationale: The ATO taxation statistics page sets out the extension periods, the tiering of the rate and the monthly declaration source, which is what distinguishes this column from the phase 1 count.
evidence_quote: The rate of payment changed in the JobKeeper extension and was split into 2 tiers.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'The number of employees that received a JK v2 payment' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not date the extension, relate the count to the tier columns, or warn about entity-level exits.

value_domain: Count of employees paid at the JobKeeper tier 1 rate
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: How many of the business's JobKeeper employees were paid at the higher extension rate, which turned on hours worked before the pandemic. The ANAO records that "Entitlement to the Tier 1 rate generally depended on whether an individual satisfied the relevant 80-hour threshold over the specified 'reference period'; otherwise, the Tier 2 rate applied", and sets the rate at $1,200 a fortnight to 3 January 2021 and $1,000 from 4 January. Read against jk2_emp_t2 it is the closest thing in the JobKeeper module to a full-time against part-time split of the subsidised workforce.
value_definition: A count of individuals at the higher of two extension rates, dollar values $1,200 then $1,000 per fortnight. The tier attaches to the employee for the whole extension rather than being reassessed each fortnight.
limitation: Eighty hours over four weeks is about twenty hours a week, measured in a fixed pre-pandemic reference period, so the split describes hours before the shock rather than hours actually worked while subsidised. The employer assessed and declared the tier itself, which makes it a self-assessment rather than a payroll fact.
rationale: The ANAO performance audit reproduces the statutory payment rates by period from section 13 of the Rules and states the 80-hour reference-period test that assigns an employee to tier 1.
evidence_quote: Entitlement to the Tier 1 rate generally depended on whether an individual satisfied the relevant 80-hour threshold over the specified 'reference period'; otherwise, the Tier 2 rate applied.
supersedes_rationale: The entry gave 'The number of employees that received a JK v2 tier 1 payment' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said what tier 1 meant, what it paid, or that the hours test looks backwards.

value_domain: Count of employees paid at the JobKeeper tier 2 rate
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: How many of the business's JobKeeper employees were paid at the lower extension rate, $750 a fortnight to 3 January 2021 and $650 from 4 January. Tier 2 is defined as a residual rather than as a category of its own: the ANAO notes that the tier 1 rate depended on meeting the 80-hour threshold in the reference period, "otherwise, the Tier 2 rate applied". Subtracting this column from jk2_emp_payment should return the tier 1 count on the same row.
value_definition: A count of individuals at the lower of the two extension rates, $750 then $650 per fortnight. It is the complement of the tier 1 count within the extension total rather than an independently assessed group.
limitation: Being a residual, it collects employees whose reference-period hours could not be established as well as genuinely short-hours staff, so it is not a clean part-time count. The two-tier design also compresses the subsidy: a person who worked 5 hours a week and one who worked 19 attract the same payment and land in the same number.
rationale: The ANAO audit gives the tier 2 rates by period from the Rules and states that tier 2 is the default where the tier 1 hours test is not met, which is what this count contains.
evidence_quote: Entitlement to the Tier 1 rate generally depended on whether an individual satisfied the relevant 80-hour threshold over the specified 'reference period'; otherwise, the Tier 2 rate applied.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'The number of employees that received a JK v2 tier 2 payment' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and did not say that tier 2 is what is left after the hours test.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in January (dollars)
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in January, which can only be January 2021 because the scheme ran from 30 March 2020. It sits at the boundary of the two extension periods: the lower rates of $1,000 and $650 a fortnight began on 4 January 2021, while the payment itself is monthly arrears, since the Rules required the Commissioner to pay no later than "14 days after the end of the calendar month in which the fortnight ends". The December claim period it mostly settles carried three fortnights rather than two.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid to the entity in the named calendar month, with no employee count, tier split or fortnight breakdown attached. It is the ATO's payment to the business, not the wages the business paid.
limitation: A January peak is a calendar artefact of the extra December fortnight, not a surge in claiming, so month-on-month comparisons across the new year mislead unless the fortnight count is held constant.
rationale: The ANAO audit sets out the statutory payment timing, the two-stage rate step-down with dates, and the fact that August and December carried three JobKeeper fortnights, which together explain what a January figure contains.
evidence_quote: The August and December 2020 net payments are higher due to three JobKeeper fortnights being included in these periods.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Disbursements in January Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so it did not fix the year, the rates in force, or the arrears timing.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in February (dollars)
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in February, necessarily February 2021 and squarely inside the final extension period. It is the first month settled wholly at the lowest rates, $1,000 for tier 1 and $650 for tier 2, which the ANAO reports as applying from 4 January 2021. Because payment ran monthly in arrears, the figure generally settles the January fortnights rather than February activity.
value_definition: A dollar amount of JobKeeper paid to the entity in the month, gross of nothing and net of any adjustments the ATO processed in that month. No tier or headcount accompanies it.
limitation: A drop between the January and February figures is mostly the extra December fortnight falling out and the January rate step-down, so reading it as employees leaving the scheme attributes an administrative change to firm behaviour.
rationale: The ANAO audit gives the extension 2 rates and their start date and sets out the monthly arrears payment rule, which is what a February amount reflects.
evidence_quote: The Commissioner must pay the jobkeeper payment no later than the later of: (a) 14 days after the end of the calendar month in which the fortnight ends
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Disbursements in February Amount' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say which rates were in force or that the payment lags the fortnights it covers.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in March (dollars)
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in March, the one month label that two scheme years can share. March 2020 carries nothing, because the ANAO records that the program "would commence on 30 March 2020, with the first payments to be received by eligible businesses in the first week of May as monthly arrears", while March 2021 is the closing month, with the last fortnight ending 28 March 2021. Any non-zero value therefore belongs to 2021 and settles February fortnights at the lowest rates.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in the named calendar month. The column names a month with no year, so the row's own reference period is what identifies which March it is.
limitation: Reading a zero as ineligibility is wrong for March 2020, when no employer was paid at all regardless of eligibility, and the scheme's final fortnight ends mid-month in 2021, so March is not a full claim month at either end.
rationale: The ANAO audit dates the scheme's start, the first payments and the final fortnight, which is what makes the March label ambiguous and its 2020 value structurally zero.
evidence_quote: the program would commence on 30 March 2020, with the first payments to be received by eligible businesses in the first week of May as monthly arrears from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Disbursements in March Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so it did not warn that two Marches share the label and that one of them cannot contain a payment.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in April (dollars)
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in April, which in practice means April 2021, the wash-up month after the scheme closed on 28 March 2021. April 2020 produced no disbursements at all: the ANAO records that the program commenced on 30 March 2020, "with the first payments to be received by eligible businesses in the first week of May as monthly arrears from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO)". An April figure therefore settles the last fortnights of the extension rather than any April activity.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid to the entity in April, drawn from the ATO's payment records rather than from the entity's accounts. It carries no fortnight or employee detail.
limitation: It cannot be used to date the start of a firm's participation, because the fortnights it pays for ended earlier and because employers who enrolled late received several fortnights at once in a single later payment.
rationale: The ANAO audit establishes when the first payments were made and the statutory 14-day-after-month-end rule, which together determine what an April amount can contain.
evidence_quote: the program would commence on 30 March 2020, with the first payments to be received by eligible businesses in the first week of May as monthly arrears from the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Disbursements in April Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not record that April 2020 is empty by construction.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in May (dollars)
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in May, which for most firms was the first JobKeeper money they ever received. Payments began in the first week of May 2020 and settled fortnights already worked back to 30 March, at a rate the ANAO states as "$1500 per fortnight per eligible employee". A May figure therefore bundles several fortnights of back pay at the flat phase 1 rate, and it is the only month in the series that behaves this way.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in May, covering more fortnights than a normal monthly payment for entities enrolled from the start of the scheme. Phase 1 had no tiers, so the amount divides by a single rate.
limitation: It is not comparable with the months around it, and dividing it by $1,500 to recover an employee count will overstate headcount by the number of backdated fortnights it contains.
rationale: The ANAO audit states when the first payments were made, that they were monthly arrears, and that the phase 1 rate was $1,500 per fortnight per eligible employee, which is what a May 2020 amount is built from.
evidence_quote: employers would receive a payment of $1500 per fortnight per eligible employee and every eligible employee must receive at least $1500 per fortnight from this business, before tax
supersedes_rationale: The entry gave 'Disbursements in May Amount' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not flag that May carries backdated fortnights and is not comparable with other months.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in June (dollars)
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in June 2020, a clean two-fortnight month at the flat phase 1 rate. Every eligible employee attracted $1,500 a fortnight regardless of hours, so the amount divides cleanly by the rate to approximate a headcount, which is not true of any extension month. June also closes the 2019-20 financial year, so it is the last month of JobKeeper falling in that year's returns.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in June at the single phase 1 rate. There is no tier split anywhere in phase 1, so no rate mix has to be assumed when interpreting the figure.
limitation: It is a reimbursement, not a measure of the firm's wage bill: the employer had to pay the employee first to meet the wage condition, and for some employees the $1,500 exceeded their ordinary wages, so part of the amount is an income transfer rather than a subsidy of pay the firm would otherwise have made.
rationale: The ANAO audit gives the phase 1 rate, the wage condition requiring employers to pay before being reimbursed, and the Treasury finding that the flat rate exceeded some individuals' ordinary wages.
evidence_quote: Requirement that employers must pay their employees first, before being reimbursed by the ATO
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Disbursements in June Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not say the payment is a reimbursement governed by the wage condition.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in July (dollars)
value_source: ANAO, Administration of the JobKeeper Scheme
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in July 2020, still under phase 1 and its flat $1,500 fortnightly rate. July is the first month of the 2020-21 financial year, so it is where a firm's JobKeeper receipts start appearing in the later year's tax and BAS columns in BLADE. As with the other phase 1 months, no tier information exists to qualify it.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in July at the flat phase 1 rate. It reflects the ATO's payment ledger for the month rather than a claim period aligned to fortnights.
limitation: The figures are net amounts, so a month can carry reversals and amendments to earlier claims: the ANAO found that 15 per cent of JobKeeper transactions by value involved manual intervention, including reversals and compliance-driven amendments. A month's total is therefore not a clean sum of that month's entitlements.
rationale: The ANAO audit describes the payment ledger, the share of transactions involving manual intervention, and what those interventions were, which is what makes a monthly figure adjustable after the fact.
evidence_quote: Manual interventions could include entering the complete transaction as the result of a telephone call, reversing or amending a transaction as a result of compliance procedures or amending a transaction at the request of the entity.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Disbursements in July Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice and gave no warning that later corrections land in a month's total.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in August (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Taxation statistics 2019-20, JobKeeper
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in August 2020, a three-fortnight month and one of the two spikes in the national series. The ATO says of its own monthly chart that "the claim periods for August and December include an extra fortnight, leading to higher net payments in those months". Everything in August was still phase 1, so the extra fortnight is worth another $1,500 per eligible employee rather than a tiered amount.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in August covering three JobKeeper fortnights rather than the usual two, at the flat phase 1 rate.
limitation: An August spike is a calendar effect and nothing else, so treating the month as evidence of deeper business distress, or annualising it, overstates the subsidy by about half.
rationale: The ATO's taxation statistics page states directly that the August claim period contains an extra fortnight and that its monthly JobKeeper figures come from business monthly declarations.
evidence_quote: In this chart, the claim periods for August and December include an extra fortnight, leading to higher net payments in those months.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Disbursements in August Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not record the extra fortnight that makes August incomparable with its neighbours.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in September (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Taxation statistics 2019-20, JobKeeper
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in September 2020, the last month dominated by the flat $1,500 rate. Phase 1 ran to 27 September and the tiered extension began the next day - the ATO dates it as "JobKeeper extension 1 - 28 September 2020 to 3 January 2021" - so the rate change lands in the final days of the month and touches only its last fortnight. September is the cleanest end point for a phase 1 series and a poor start point for an extension one.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in September, almost entirely at the phase 1 rate with at most the beginning of one extension fortnight inside it.
limitation: Because the month straddles the rate change, dividing it by any single fortnightly rate to recover an employee count gives a wrong answer; the tier columns exist for the extension precisely because a single rate no longer applies after 27 September.
rationale: The ATO taxation statistics page dates phase 1 to 27 September 2020 and the first extension from 28 September 2020, which places the rate change inside this month.
evidence_quote: JobKeeper extension 1 - 28 September 2020 to 3 January 2021
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Disbursements in September Amount' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not identify September as the month the rate structure changed.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in October (dollars)
value_source: ATO media release, Time for employers to get ready for the JobKeeper extension
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in October 2020, the first month of the extension and the month the scheme's population was re-tested. The ATO told employers to complete their October declarations "between 1 - 14 October 2020 ... to receive your reimbursement for the September fortnights", and separately to submit an actual decline in turnover test before 31 October. So the October amount still settles September fortnights while the eligibility of the business itself was being re-established.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in October, generally in respect of September fortnights, at the phase 1 rate for fortnights ending before 28 September and at tier rates after it.
limitation: A business that disappears from the series after October failed the actual decline in turnover retest rather than losing its employees, so a zero from this month on is an entity eligibility outcome and must not be read as a fall in employment.
rationale: The ATO media release sets out the October declaration window, the fortnights it reimburses and the actual decline in turnover test that had to be passed during the same month.
evidence_quote: Between 1 - 14 October 2020: complete your October JobKeeper monthly business declarations to receive your reimbursement for the September fortnights.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Disbursements in October Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not mention the turnover retest that determines who remains in the series after October.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in November (dollars)
value_source: ATO media release, Time for employers to get ready for the JobKeeper extension
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in November 2020, the first month whose claim carried a confirmed tier for every employee. The ATO required that "From 1 November 2020: complete your monthly business declaration and confirm what payment tier you are claiming for each employee", so November is where the tier split behind the amount becomes reliable. The payment itself covers October fortnights at the extension rates of $1,200 and $750.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in November under extension 1 rates, reflecting a mix of tier 1 and tier 2 employees that the employer confirmed in its declaration.
limitation: The tier mix behind the amount is the employer's own assessment of each employee's reference-period hours, not a payroll measurement, so two firms with identical rosters can produce different amounts through different judgements about the 80-hour test.
rationale: The ATO media release states the date from which employers had to confirm the payment tier for each employee in the monthly business declaration, which is what the November payment reflects.
evidence_quote: From 1 November 2020: complete your monthly business declaration and confirm what payment tier you are claiming for each employee.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Disbursements in November Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so it did not connect the amount to the newly confirmed tier reporting.

value_domain: JobKeeper amount disbursed to the business in December (dollars)
value_source: ATO, Taxation statistics 2019-20, JobKeeper
variable_description: The JobKeeper money the ATO paid this business in December 2020, the second and last three-fortnight month of the scheme. The ATO notes that "the claim periods for August and December include an extra fortnight, leading to higher net payments in those months", and unlike August the extra fortnight here is paid at extension 1 tier rates of $1,200 and $750 rather than a flat rate. It is the final month before the rates stepped down again on 4 January 2021.
value_definition: A dollar amount paid in December covering three JobKeeper fortnights at extension 1 tier rates, with no split by tier in the column itself.
limitation: Comparing December with January confounds two changes at once - the extra fortnight dropping out and the rate step-down on 4 January - so the fall between them cannot be attributed to either without holding the fortnight count fixed.
rationale: The ATO taxation statistics page states that the December claim period contains an extra fortnight and dates extension 2 from 4 January 2021, which is what makes the December to January comparison ambiguous.
evidence_quote: In this chart, the claim periods for August and December include an extra fortnight, leading to higher net payments in those months.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Disbursements in December Amount' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it did not record the extra fortnight or the rate change that follows it.

value_domain: BLADE integration version identifier for the JobKeeper module
value_source: ABS, Business Longitudinal Analysis Data Environment (BLADE)
variable_description: Which ABS integration run produced this JobKeeper row, an internal reference to the build rather than anything about the payment. The ABS lists the JobKeeper Payment Scheme among the ATO sources it brings into BLADE, and this code identifies the extract of that source and the linkage to the business spine that produced the row. Rows from different runs describe the same scheme but not necessarily the same figures.
value_definition: An alphanumeric code identifying the integration run, constant within a build of the JobKeeper module and carrying no date component.
limitation: It cannot tell you when the ATO data were extracted relative to the ATO's own compliance work, which matters here more than in most modules: JobKeeper amounts were amended and reversed after the fact, so two versions can disagree about the same ABN's payments without either being wrong.
rationale: No published ABS documentation of the BLADE integration version codes could be fetched; the reading rests on the data item list label, on the same column appearing in other BLADE modules, and on the ABS BLADE page naming the JobKeeper Payment Scheme as an ATO input.
evidence_quote: Australian Taxation Office: Business Activity Statements (BAS), Business Income Tax (BIT) filings, Pay as You Go (PAYG) summaries, Single Touch Payroll (STP), JobKeeper Payment Scheme, JobMaker Hiring Credit Scheme, Capital Gains Tax (CGT) and Consolidated Groups
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Integration version of dataset (internal ABS reference)' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so it did not warn that payment figures can differ between versions.

value_domain: ABS integration version stamp on the JobMaker Hiring Credit table
value_source: ATO, JobMaker Hiring Credit scheme
variable_description: Which ABS build of the JobMaker Hiring Credit extract this row came from, not anything about the firm's hiring. The scheme itself was short and closed: employers could claim for eligible additional employees hired between 7 October 2020 and 6 October 2021, and the last claim period ended on 31 January 2023. Two rows for the same business carrying different stamps are two loads of the same administrative source, not two separate claims.
value_definition: An alphanumeric label identifying the integration run, in the same style as the key_version and frame_version stamps on other BLADE tables. It has no units and no meaningful order.
limitation: It cannot date a claim or identify a JobMaker period. Grouping on it counts ABS processing runs rather than employers, and a change of stamp between releases is not evidence that the underlying ATO data changed.
rationale: The ATO page fixes what the JobMaker Hiring Credit table records and the window it covers. The version column itself is described only as an internal ABS reference and no published page documents it, so the reading here is inferred from the identical stamps carried by other BLADE tables.
evidence_quote: Eligible employers could access the JobMaker Hiring Credit for each eligible additional employee they hired between 7 October 2020 and 6 October 2021.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's wording, 'Integration version of dataset (internal ABS reference)', with the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation, so nothing said that the column is extract metadata rather than a measure of the firm.

value_domain: Job-sharing clause flag on a federal enterprise agreement
value_source: DEWR, Workplace Agreements Database
variable_description: Whether the federal enterprise agreement contains a job-sharing arrangement, or a promise to introduce or discuss one during the agreement's life. The row is an agreement, not a business: DEWR codes about 200 items from the text of each lodged agreement, and the department says the database holds "conditions information for all federal enterprise agreements approved since 1 January 1997". A BLADE user therefore reads this as a term the parties wrote down, joined to the employer, rather than as a workplace practice observed by anyone.
value_definition: A single-character flag. Y marks an agreement carrying the clause; anything else, blank included, means no clause was coded. There is no distinct code meaning the coder considered the question and found nothing.
limitation: A clause is not a practice, and no employee need ever job-share for the flag to be set. A commitment merely to discuss job sharing is counted the same as an operating arrangement. Agreements approved before 1 January 1997 carry no conditions coding at all, so an empty flag in the early years is a coverage gap rather than a workplace without job sharing.
rationale: The DEWR page is the custodian's own description of the Workplace Agreements Database: what it contains, from when, that around 200 data items are recorded per agreement, and that a subset of it is the BLADE module. That establishes the unit of observation and the coding basis, which is what the flag's meaning turns on.
evidence_quote: The database contains wage information for all federal enterprise agreements since the introduction of enterprise bargaining in October 1991, and conditions information for all federal enterprise agreements approved since 1 January 1997.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's long clause definition as its description and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it never said that the unit is an agreement, that the flag is coded from text by DEWR, or that the conditions coding starts only in 1997.

value_domain: Jury service make-up pay clause flag on a federal enterprise agreement
value_source: Fair Work Ombudsman, Jury duty
variable_description: Whether the enterprise agreement promises to pay the gap between an employee's jury service payment and their ordinary wage. That gap has a statutory name: under the National Employment Standards "the employer only needs to pay them 'make-up pay' for the first 10 days that they're absent from work". Because the standard made make-up pay a minimum entitlement, DEWR only codes this item for agreements made before 1 January 2011, so the column is a closed series rather than a running one.
value_definition: A single-character flag, Y where the clause is present. It is coded only for agreements made before 1 January 2011, so after that date the column is empty by rule rather than by observation.
limitation: A blank after 2010 does not mean employers stopped paying. The entitlement became a statutory minimum, agreements no longer needed a clause, and DEWR stopped coding one, so a falling count of Y flags measures a change in the coding rule and in the law, not a fall in employer generosity. The flag also cannot tell you whether the agreement was more generous than the standard, for instance by covering casuals or by running past ten days.
rationale: The Fair Work Ombudsman page defines make-up pay for jury duty in the terms the WAD label uses - the difference between the court's payment and the employee's base rate for the ordinary hours they would have worked - and dates it to the National Employment Standards, which is what explains the pre-2011 coding cut-off recorded in the BLADE metadata.
evidence_quote: If the employee does provide this evidence when asked, the employer only needs to pay them 'make-up pay' for the first 10 days that they're absent from work.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated the custodian's clause wording and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence, leaving the pre-2011 coding note unexplained and inviting a reader to treat the drop-off as a change in employer behaviour.

value_domain: Count of beef cattle on the holding
value_source: ABS, Australian Agriculture: Livestock methodology, 2022-23
variable_description: How many beef cattle the farm business had on hand: a stock held at a point in time, not turn-off over the year. ABS agricultural collections count animals at the end of the financial year - "Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June." - and this is the herd that carries into the following season. Unlike the dairy items beside it, the label on this column does not name a date, so it should be read as the same 30 June count unless a specific year's collection says otherwise.
value_definition: A whole-number count of animals of all ages, not a value, a weight or a stocking rate. It is one of the livestock holding items the Farm-level Longitudinal Agricultural Dataset carries for each farm business and year.
limitation: A herd is not production. Numbers can sit flat while turn-off rises or falls, and a business running agisted cattle it does not own can report animals that belong to someone else. Farms below the ABS collection threshold are absent altogether, so small cattle holdings never enter the column.
rationale: The ABS livestock methodology states the reference point for every livestock holding count in its agricultural collections, which are the collections the Farm-level Longitudinal Agricultural Dataset is built from.
evidence_quote: Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Total beef cattle on hand' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so nothing told a reader it is a closing stock rather than a flow, or that it is a count rather than a value.

value_domain: Count of dairy cows on the holding at 30 June
value_source: ABS, Australian Agriculture: Livestock methodology, 2022-23
variable_description: How many dairy cows the farm held at 30 June - the milking herd as a closing stock, not an average across the year. The ABS anchors all its livestock holding counts to that date: "Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June." Adding this column to k_dairy_other gives the whole dairy herd, since this one covers producing cows and the other covers everything else.
value_definition: A whole-number count of cows, not litres and not a value. It is a livestock holding item in the Farm-level Longitudinal Agricultural Dataset, reported per farm business per year.
limitation: A cow count is not milk output. Yield per cow roughly doubled over the decades this panel spans, so a shrinking herd can sit behind rising production. The 30 June point also falls at different stages of the calving cycle in different regions, which makes cross-regional herd comparisons at a single date less like for like than they appear.
rationale: The ABS livestock methodology gives the 30 June reference point that the column's own label names, and separates cows in milk and dry from other dairy cattle, which is the split between this column and k_dairy_other.
evidence_quote: Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Dairy cows on hand (30 June)' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, and gave a reader no way to see that it pairs with k_dairy_other to make the full herd.

value_domain: Count of dairy cattle other than cows on the holding at 30 June
value_source: ABS, Australian Agriculture: Livestock methodology, 2022-23
variable_description: How many dairy cattle other than milking cows the farm held at 30 June - heifers, calves and bulls being reared as herd replacements. It is the replacement pipeline rather than the producing herd, so a business expanding its dairy will show this column rising before k_dairy_cows does. The ABS counts all livestock holdings at the same point: "Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June."
value_definition: A whole-number count of animals. It is defined by exclusion - dairy cattle that are not counted as cows - so its content depends on where the collection drew the cow boundary in a given year.
limitation: Used alone it understates the dairy operation, and used as 'dairy cattle' it is wrong in the other direction because the milking herd is not in it. A high ratio to k_dairy_cows can mean planned expansion or simply a young herd after a cull, and the column cannot separate the two.
rationale: The ABS livestock methodology sets the 30 June reference and distinguishes dairy cattle in milk and dry from the rest of the dairy herd, which is exactly the split this residual column completes.
evidence_quote: Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'All other dairy cattle on hand (30 June)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing explained that the column is a residual defined against k_dairy_cows.

value_domain: Count of sheep excluding lambs on the holding at 30 June
value_source: ABS, Australian Agriculture: Livestock methodology, 2022-23
variable_description: How many sheep the farm held at 30 June, counting adult sheep only - the label puts lambs outside the column. That exclusion matters at that date, because in most Australian systems the current drop is still on the ground in June, so this figure sits well below any full flock count. The ABS anchors the count to the year end: "Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June."
value_definition: A whole-number count of adult sheep, excluding lambs, held on the farm at 30 June. It is a head count, not a dry sheep equivalent and not a wool clip.
limitation: It is not the flock. Because lambs are excluded, a farm with a strong lambing looks the same size here as one with none, and a lamb-producing enterprise is systematically understated relative to a wool wether flock. The column also cannot separate breeding ewes from wethers, which is the split that drives whether the business sells wool or meat.
rationale: The ABS livestock methodology gives the 30 June reference point that the column's label names, and the label itself carries the lamb exclusion that governs how the number should be read.
evidence_quote: Livestock herd refers to livestock on holding at 30 June.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Sheep on hand (excluding lambs) (30 June)' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader had no warning that the exclusion of lambs makes this much smaller than a flock count.

value_domain: Area of holding in hectares
value_source: ABS, Agricultural Commodities, Australia methodology, 2020-21
variable_description: The total area of land the agricultural business operated, in hectares - the area of holding, not the area actually cropped or grazed. It is the standard size measure in the Farm-level Longitudinal Agricultural Dataset and sits beside the crop and livestock items as a farm characteristic. The businesses it covers are limited by the ABS collection threshold: a business was in scope only where "the estimated value of their agricultural operations (EVAO) was $40,000 or greater".
value_definition: A hectare figure covering the whole holding at the reference date, owned and leased land together. It is an area only, so an irrigated orchard block and a pastoral lease are measured on the same scale.
limitation: It cannot stand in for farm size in economic terms. A 50 hectare orchard can out-earn a 50,000 hectare pastoral run, and the column says nothing about land quality, water access or how much of the holding was in use. Land run under agistment or short-term arrangements may fall inside one business's return and outside the other's, so the areas of two linked businesses need not add to the land they jointly work.
rationale: The ABS agricultural commodities methodology sets the scope, the unit and the collection method for the census and survey data that the Farm-level Longitudinal Agricultural Dataset is assembled from, which is what bounds who has an area of holding recorded at all. No published page gives a verbatim definition of the area of holding item, so the reading of the item itself is assembled rather than quoted.
evidence_quote: Businesses on the Australian Bureau of Statistics' Business Register (ABSBR) were in scope for the 2020-21 Agricultural Census if: they undertook agricultural activity, and the estimated value of their agricultural operations (EVAO) was $40,000 or greater
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Total land area (area of holding)' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so nothing warned a reader that area is a poor proxy for economic scale or that small holdings are out of scope entirely.

value_domain: Count of almond trees of bearing age
value_source: ABARES, Agricultural Data Integration Project
variable_description: The number of almond trees on the holding that had reached bearing age, and so could contribute to that season's crop. Almonds are grown on a small number of large irrigated plantings in the Murray-Darling, so this count is concentrated in few businesses and steps up when a whole new orchard reaches maturity rather than drifting. The count comes from the ABS agricultural collections that the Farm-level Longitudinal Agricultural Dataset is assembled from, which asked growers to report bearing and non-bearing trees separately.
value_definition: A whole-number count of individual trees, not an area and not a tonnage. It is the bearing half of a pair: the same crop's non-bearing count sits in the matching k_tree_nonbear_ column, and the two together give the total planting.
limitation: It cannot tell you yield. Tree counts say nothing about spacing, variety, water allocation or nut set, and a farm with more trees can produce less in a dry allocation year. Farms below the ABS scope threshold never enter the collection, so the column describes commercial plantings only.

value_domain: Scrip-for-scrip roll-over chosen indicator
value_source: ATO, Guide to capital gains tax 2023, Investments in shares and units
variable_description: Whether the entity chose scrip-for-scrip roll-over on shares or units it gave up in a takeover or merger during the year. Choosing it defers rather than removes the tax: "The rollover allows you to disregard the capital gain made from the original shares, units or other interest. You are taken to have acquired the replacement shares, units or other interest for the cost base of the original interest." This was label A of Part K of the old capital gains tax schedule, which the current schedule no longer carries.
value_definition: A single character. Y is yes and N is no, and the metadata treats everything else as an invalid or absent response, so the column is effectively three-valued.
limitation: A Y is a self-assessed choice, not a ruling. The entity works out for itself whether the 80 per cent acquisition test and the other Subdivision 124-M conditions were met, and the ATO can disagree later. A blank does not mean no takeover: it can mean the entity was ineligible, made a loss rather than a gain, or lodged no schedule at all because its total capital gains and losses were under the $10,000 threshold.
rationale: The ATO guide defines the scrip-for-scrip roll-over, the conditions on it and its effect on the cost base, and the archived CGT schedule shows this as label A of the schedule's Part K, which is what the variable name and the OF prefix encode.
evidence_quote: The rollover allows you to disregard the capital gain made from the original shares, units or other interest.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the bare old-form label 'OF: Roll-over chosen?' with the generic no-value-list sentence printed twice, so nothing said which schedule part it came from, what choosing the roll-over does, or that the item no longer exists on the current form.

value_domain: Cost base of original interests given up, dollars
value_source: ATO, Guide to capital gains tax 2023, Investments in shares and units
variable_description: The cost base of the shares or units the entity handed over in a scrip-for-scrip exchange, in dollars. It is what the entity had in the interests it gave up, and under the roll-over it carries across to the new holding: "You are taken to have acquired the replacement shares, units or other interest for the cost base of the original interest." Set against label C, the market value of what came back, the gap is the gain the roll-over defers. The OF prefix on the BLADE label is the old-form wording: this was label B of Part K of the CGT schedule, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for exchanging taxpayer", which the current schedule no longer carries.
value_definition: A whole-dollar amount reported on the schedule. It is a cost base, so it includes the acquisition cost and the other cost base elements rather than the purchase price alone.
limitation: It is neither the gain nor the proceeds. A large cost base can accompany a small gain or a loss, and the roll-over is not available for a loss at all. Where only part of the exchange qualified, the cost base has to be apportioned between the replacement interest and the cash, and this column does not record how much went to each.
rationale: The ATO guide states the cost base transfer that gives this label its meaning, and the archived CGT schedule places it as label B of Part K, beside the replacement market value and the cash consideration that complete the exchange.
evidence_quote: You are taken to have acquired the replacement shares, units or other interest for the cost base of the original interest.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Original interests cost base' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader could not tell whose cost base it is, which side of the exchange it sits on, or that it is not a gain.

value_domain: Market value of replacement interests received, dollars
value_source: ATO, Guide to capital gains tax 2023, Investments in shares and units
variable_description: The market value of the shares or units the entity received in place of the ones it gave up, in dollars. Value is struck immediately after the exchange, the same point the ATO uses in its fallback rule for pre-CGT holdings, where "the cost base of the replacement interest is its market value just after the acquisition". Together with the original cost base at label B it brackets the gain the roll-over defers. The OF prefix on the BLADE label is the old-form wording: this was label C of Part K of the CGT schedule, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for exchanging taxpayer", which the current schedule no longer carries.
value_definition: A dollar amount for the value of the replacement interests, not a number of shares. Where the takeover consideration was part scrip and part cash, only the scrip part is here; the cash sits at label D.
limitation: A takeover market value is an estimate, usually a listed price on one day, so it is not a realised amount and small timing differences move it. It cannot be used as a measure of deal size across the population either, because entities whose total capital gains and losses were $10,000 or less lodged no schedule and appear nowhere.
rationale: The ATO guide fixes the valuation point for a replacement interest in a scrip-for-scrip exchange, and the archived CGT schedule places this as label C of Part K, directly beside the original cost base it is compared against.
evidence_quote: However, if the arrangement is one that would otherwise qualify for a scrip for scrip rollover, the cost base of the replacement interest is its market value just after the acquisition.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Replacement interests market value' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said when the value is struck, that it excludes any cash in the deal, or how it relates to the cost base column beside it.

value_domain: Cash and other non-scrip consideration received, dollars
value_source: ATO, Guide to capital gains tax 2023, Investments in shares and units
variable_description: The cash and other non-scrip consideration the entity received in the exchange - the part of the deal no roll-over can cover. A figure here is the marker of a partial roll-over: "You may only be eligible for a partial rollover if you exchange shares, units or interests for similar interests in another entity (replacement interest) plus something else, usually cash." The gain on that slice is taxed in the year of the exchange rather than deferred. The OF prefix on the BLADE label is the old-form wording: this was label D of Part K of the CGT schedule, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for exchanging taxpayer", which the current schedule no longer carries.
value_definition: A dollar amount covering cash and any other consideration that is not a replacement interest. A zero or a blank means the exchange was pure scrip.
limitation: It is consideration received, not the taxable gain on it. The cost base of the original interest is apportioned first, so a large cash figure can carry a small gain, and the column does not record the apportionment. It also does not identify what the 'other' consideration was where it was not cash.
rationale: The ATO guide defines the partial roll-over that a non-scrip component triggers and sets out the apportionment it requires, and the archived CGT schedule places this as label D of Part K alongside the cost base and market value labels.
evidence_quote: You may only be eligible for a partial rollover if you exchange shares, units or interests for similar interests in another entity (replacement interest) plus something else, usually cash.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Cash and other considerations' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing explained that a non-zero value signals a partial roll-over or that the amount is not itself taxable.

value_domain: Acquiring entity indicator on the scrip-for-scrip schedule
value_source: ATO, Capital gains tax (CGT) schedule 2005
variable_description: Whether the entity was the acquirer in a scrip-for-scrip arrangement rather than a target holder giving interests up. It is the gate on a whole block of the old schedule, headed "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for acquiring entity - to be completed by companies and trusts only", so a Y here changes what the other l_scrpt_ columns on the row describe. Partnerships and superannuation funds never completed that part, which is why a blank carries no information about them.
value_definition: A single character, Y or N, with anything else treated as an invalid or absent response.
limitation: It marks a role in one arrangement, not a corporate status: the same company can be an acquirer one year and a target holder the next, and an acquirer need have no capital gain of its own. Because the schedule was lodged only where total capital gains or losses exceeded $10,000, small acquirers are missing entirely, so this is not a census of takeover activity.
rationale: The archived CGT schedule shows Part L in full, including its heading restricting the part to companies and trusts and its label E, which is what the variable name encodes and what determines when the rest of the l_scrpt_ family is populated.
evidence_quote: Part L Scrip-for-scrip rollover for acquiring entity - to be completed by companies and trusts only
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Acquiring entity?' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader had no way to know that the flag governs a whole block of columns or that two entity types never complete it.

value_domain: Count of original entities in the arrangement
value_source: ATO, Guide to capital gains tax 2023, Investments in shares and units
variable_description: How many original entities - the target companies or trusts - the acquirer took interests in under the arrangement. Each has to satisfy a control test for the roll-over to be available at all, since a roll-over "is only available if the exchange is in consequence of an arrangement that results in the acquiring entity (or the wholly owned group of which it is a member) becoming the owner of 80% or more of the original company or trust". A figure above one therefore marks a multi-target restructure rather than a single takeover. The OF prefix marks the old-form wording: this was label F of Part L, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for acquiring entity - to be completed by companies and trusts only".
value_definition: A three-digit count, so it cannot exceed 999. It counts entities, not holders or interests, so a takeover of one company with thousands of shareholders is a 1.
limitation: It says nothing about the size of the targets or how much of each was acquired, so a 1 can be a billion-dollar takeover and a 12 a small internal reorganisation. It also does not identify the targets: the schedule put their tax file numbers at the adjacent label G, which BLADE does not carry.
rationale: The ATO guide states the 80 per cent ownership test that applies to each original entity, which is what makes a count of them meaningful, and the archived CGT schedule places this as label F of Part L beside the target identifier the dataset omits.
evidence_quote: A rollover is only available if the exchange is in consequence of an arrangement that results in the acquiring entity (or the wholly owned group of which it is a member) becoming the owner of 80% or more of the original company or trust.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Number of original entities' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said what an original entity is, that the count tops out at three digits, or that the targets themselves are not identified.

value_domain: Other consideration given by the acquiring entity, dollars
value_source: ATO, Guide to capital gains tax 2023, Investments in shares and units
variable_description: The cash and other non-scrip consideration the acquirer gave to target holders, in dollars. It is the acquirer's mirror of the cash column on the exchanging taxpayer's side, and its presence is what limits those holders to a partial roll-over, because "the rollover applies only to the replacement interest". The OF prefix marks the old-form wording: this was label J of Part L, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for acquiring entity - to be completed by companies and trusts only".
value_definition: An eleven-digit dollar amount, so it accommodates deals up to roughly a hundred billion dollars. It is the amount given, not the amount over which roll-over was obtained.
limitation: It is not the price of the deal. The scrip half of the consideration is absent, and the schedule's counts of shares and options issued at labels H and I are not carried in BLADE, so total consideration cannot be rebuilt from what is here. A zero means a pure scrip offer, not a free acquisition.
rationale: The ATO guide explains why non-scrip consideration restricts the roll-over to the replacement interest, which is what a figure in this column implies for the target holders, and the archived schedule places it as label J of Part L next to the share and option counts BLADE omits.
evidence_quote: This is because the rollover applies only to the replacement interest.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Amount of other considerations' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader could not tell whose consideration it is, that it excludes the scrip, or that the companion counts are missing from the dataset.

value_domain: First element of cost base of interests acquired, dollars
value_source: ATO Legal database, Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 section 124-782
variable_description: The cost base the acquirer took on for the interests it acquired, in dollars, where the roll-over passed the target holder's cost base straight across. The transfer is statutory: "The cost base of an original interest acquired by an acquiring entity under the arrangement from an original interest holder becomes the first element of the cost base and reduced cost base of the acquiring entity for the interest" where the holder obtains a roll-over and is a significant or common stakeholder. The figure is therefore inherited, not paid. The OF prefix marks the old-form wording: this was label K of Part L, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for acquiring entity - to be completed by companies and trusts only".
value_definition: A dollar amount and a first element of cost base only, so later cost base elements are outside it. It applies to the interests the acquirer received, not to the shares it issued.
limitation: It is not what the acquirer paid. A low figure on a large takeover reflects a long-held, low-cost target holding rather than a bargain, and it stores a larger gain for the acquirer on any later disposal. Interests for which no roll-over was chosen fall outside the transfer rule and are costed the ordinary way, so the column does not cover the whole acquisition.
rationale: Section 124-782 of the Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 is the provision this label reports against, and the ATO legal database publishes its text, including the condition that the holder be a significant or common stakeholder. The archived schedule places the label as K of Part L.
evidence_quote: The cost base of an original interest acquired by an acquiring entity under the arrangement from an original interest holder becomes the first element of the cost base and reduced cost base of the acquiring entity for the interest
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: First element of cost base of interests acquired' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said the amount is transferred from the seller rather than paid, or which interests it covers.

value_domain: Joint choice for scrip-for-scrip roll-over indicator
value_source: ATO, Class Ruling CR 2001/5, Income tax: capital gains: scrip for scrip roll-over
variable_description: Whether the acquirer joined the target holder in choosing the roll-over, which the law requires only where a significant or common stakeholder is involved. The ATO puts the trigger plainly: "Paragraph 124-780(3)(d) provides that roll-over is available for an interest holder that is a significant or common stakeholder only if the replacement entity (Defiance) jointly elects for roll-over." A Y therefore signals a concentrated-ownership deal rather than a public takeover. The OF prefix marks the old-form wording: this was label L of Part L, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for acquiring entity - to be completed by companies and trusts only".
value_definition: A single character, Y or N, with anything else invalid or absent. It is a procedural election, not an amount.
limitation: A blank is the ordinary case, not a refusal: a widely held takeover has no significant or common stakeholder, so no joint choice is needed and nothing is reported, and reading blanks as the acquirer declining inverts the meaning. Note also that the BLADE metadata tags this item to superannuation, which is a mis-tag - it is a capital gains item on the CGT schedule.
rationale: The class ruling states the paragraph of Subdivision 124-M that makes the acquirer's joint election a condition of the roll-over for stakeholders, and defines the significant and common stakeholder tests that decide when the label is used at all.
evidence_quote: Paragraph 124-780(3)(d) provides that roll-over is available for an interest holder that is a significant or common stakeholder only if the replacement entity (Defiance) jointly elects for roll-over.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Joint choice for rollover' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader had no way to know that a blank is normal, or why a joint election is needed in some deals and not others.

value_domain: Cost base of significant or common stakeholder interests acquired, dollars
value_source: ATO, Class Ruling CR 2001/5, Income tax: capital gains: scrip for scrip roll-over
variable_description: The cost base the acquirer took on for interests acquired from a significant or common stakeholder, in dollars. It isolates the slice of the acquisition where the cost base transfer rule bites, since "An interest holder is a significant stakeholder for an arrangement if it had a significant stake (30%) in the original entity before the arrangement and in the replacement entity after the arrangement". A figure here means concentrated ownership sat on both sides of the deal. The OF prefix marks the old-form wording: this was label M of Part L, "Scrip-for-scrip rollover for acquiring entity - to be completed by companies and trusts only".
value_definition: A dollar amount and a cost base rather than a payment, restricted to interests acquired from holders who met the significant or common stakeholder test.
limitation: It is a subset, so adding it to the whole-deal cost base at label K double counts. A zero does not prove no concentrated holder existed: it can mean the holder did not obtain a roll-over, or that the original or replacement entity had at least 300 members, which rules out a common stakeholder by definition.
rationale: The class ruling defines both the significant stakeholder test and the 300-member carve-out for common stakeholders, which is what determines whether this label is populated, and the archived schedule shows it as the final label of Part L.
evidence_quote: An interest holder is a significant stakeholder for an arrangement if it had a significant stake (30%) in the original entity before the arrangement and in the replacement entity after the arrangement: subsection 124-783(1).
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'OF: Cost base - significant common stakeholder interests acquired' with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing defined a stakeholder, explained why the slice is reported separately, or warned against adding it to the neighbouring total.

value_domain: ABS integration version stamp on the ABN-to-unit key table
value_source: ABS, ANZSIC 2006 (Revision 2.0), Appendix 1 Australian units model
variable_description: Which ABS integration run produced this ABN-to-unit mapping, rather than a fact about any business. The table it sits on is BLADE's bridge from a de-identified ABN to the statistical unit, and it is needed because the two do not line up one to one: the ABS defines the Type of Activity Unit as "a producing unit comprising one or more legal entities, sub-entities or branches of a legal entity that can report productive and employment activities via a minimum set of data items", which is why the same table carries many_abn_to_one_tau and one_abn_to_many_tau flags. This column says which build of that mapping you are reading.
value_definition: A short alphanumeric string in the style of the example given in the metadata, an integration number with a version suffix. It is a label, not a quantity, and its order carries no meaning.
limitation: It cannot date the mapping or detect a change in a business. Rows that differ only in this stamp are the same ABN-to-unit relationship recorded in two ABS builds, so treating it as a panel dimension inflates counts of businesses and of links.
rationale: The ABS units model page defines the Type of Activity Unit and the Enterprise Group that this key table maps ABNs onto, which is what gives the table its purpose. The version column itself is documented only as an internal ABS reference, so the reading of it is inferred from the matching stamps on other BLADE tables.
evidence_quote: The Type of Activity Unit (TAU) is a producing unit comprising one or more legal entities, sub-entities or branches of a legal entity that can report productive and employment activities via a minimum set of data items.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Integration version (internal ABS reference)' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so nothing said what the table it stamps is for or warned against treating the stamp as a dimension.

value_domain: Austrade Key Account client flag
value_source: ABS, Business Longitudinal Analysis Data Environment (BLADE)
variable_description: Whether Austrade treated the business as a Key Account client in that financial year, its most intensive category of exporter support. The Microdata on Australian Exporters panel is Austrade's own client record integrated into BLADE, carried one row per de-identified ABN per financial year, so this is an agency service flag rather than a survey answer or a tax item. The custodian notes the service was renamed after 2022-23, which means this column and the excelerate flag on the same row describe near-identical client groups under two names.
value_definition: A binary indicator, 1 for yes and 0 for no, recorded per business per financial year. It comes from Austrade's client management system rather than from a collection.
limitation: It measures Austrade's attention, not the firm's exports. A business can export heavily and never be a Key Account, and selection into the category is deliberate, so comparing flagged against unflagged firms on export growth measures who Austrade chose at least as much as what the service did. The rename also breaks the series at 2022-23 unless excelerate is used for the earlier years.
rationale: The ABS BLADE page confirms that Austrade's Microdata on Australian Exporters is one of the integrated sources and fixes the business as the unit. Austrade does not publish a definition of its Key Account client category, so what the flag marks is taken from the custodian's own note in the BLADE metadata rather than from a fetchable Austrade page.
evidence_quote: The Business Longitudinal Analysis Data Environment (BLADE) is an economic data tool combining tax, trade and intellectual property data with information from ABS surveys to provide a better understanding of the Australian economy and businesses performance over time.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's parenthetical note about the service rename as its whole description, with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said the flag is an agency service record or warned about the selection problem it creates.

value_domain: Austrade Landing Pads programme participation flag
value_source: Austrade, Landing Pads
variable_description: Whether the business took part in Austrade's Landing Pads programme in that financial year. Austrade describes the programme narrowly: "We help export-ready Australian tech businesses to expand globally and find international investors." Applicants must already have a product with customers or partners and at least twelve months of funding runway, so the flag marks a screened and selected group rather than any firm that wanted help.
value_definition: A binary indicator, 1 for yes and 0 for no, recorded per de-identified business per financial year on the Microdata on Australian Exporters panel.
limitation: Participation is applied for and selected, so a flag here cannot be read as the cause of later export growth: the eligibility bar already screens for firms that were expanding anyway. The column also says nothing about which market the business went to, how long the placement ran, or whether any deal followed.
rationale: The Austrade programme page is the custodian's own description of what Landing Pads is, who it targets and what an applicant must already have, which is what the participation flag records and what makes the selection problem visible.
evidence_quote: We help export-ready Australian tech businesses to expand globally and find international investors.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's one-line label with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said what the programme is, that participation is selective, or why that matters for anyone using the flag as a treatment.

value_domain: ANZSIC 2006 industry class code
value_source: ABS, ANZSIC 2006 (Revision 2.0), Numbering system and titles
variable_description: The most recent four-digit ANZSIC 2006 industry class the ABS held for the business, carried unchanged on every year of its record. It is a fixed attribute, unlike cast_anzsic06 and d_anzsic06 on the same row, which give the industry as it stood in that year. The classification's own convention matters when reading the codes: "Use of a nine in the fourth digit of the code designates a residual class."
value_definition: A four-digit ANZSIC 2006 class code. Both 0 and 9999 mean unknown or missing, while a real code ending in nine marks an 'other' class within its group, so 9999 is a missing-value code and not a class.
limitation: It is a fixed attribute, not a history. Splitting a panel on it assigns the business's final industry to all its earlier years, which back-dates every reclassification - a genuine change of activity and an ABS coding correction alike - and makes industry switching invisible. Use cast_anzsic06 or d_anzsic06 where the industry in the year of the row is what matters.
rationale: The ABS numbering page is the classification publisher's own account of the code structure, including the residual-class convention that governs how a four-digit value should be read, and the ANZSIC 2006 edition is the one the column names.
evidence_quote: Use of a nine in the fourth digit of the code designates a residual class.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's label and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing distinguished the 'latest' column from the year-specific industry columns beside it or explained the 9999 code.

value_domain: ANZSIC 2006 industry division
value_source: ABS, ANZSIC 2006 (Revision 2.0), Division definitions
variable_description: The most recent ANZSIC 2006 division for the business, the single-letter top level of the industry classification, held constant across its record. A division is a broad grouping of activity rather than a product: division A, for example, "includes units mainly engaged in growing crops, raising animals, growing and harvesting timber, and harvesting fish and other animals from farms or their natural habitats". Its sibling d_div06 gives the division in the year of the row, derived from that year's class code.
value_definition: A single alphabetic character, the leading character of the ANZSIC 2006 code. It is derived from the class code rather than collected, so it can never disagree with the class it came from.
limitation: Nineteen divisions is a very coarse cut, and controlling on it absorbs almost none of the within-industry variation that a productivity or firm-dynamics study cares about: manufacturing covers food processing and aircraft assembly on the same letter. Like latest_anzsic06 it is the final division rather than the division in the year of the row.
rationale: The ABS division definitions page is the classification publisher's own statement of what each division covers, which is the level this column reports, and the ANZSIC 2006 edition is the one the column names.
evidence_quote: The Agriculture, Forestry and Fishing Division includes units mainly engaged in growing crops, raising animals, growing and harvesting timber, and harvesting fish and other animals from farms or their natural habitats.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's label with a single division code as its valid-response text and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so nothing said that the division is derived from the class or that it is fixed rather than annual.

value_domain: SISCA 2008 institutional sector code
value_source: ABS, Standard Economic Sector Classifications of Australia (SESCA), 2008 (Version 1.1)
variable_description: The most recent SISCA 2008 institutional sector for the unit, the code that separates corporations, financial corporations, government and households. The ABS defines the classification as "a classification of institutional units which provides a framework for dividing the Australian economy into institutional sectors" grouping units of similar economic function and structure. Its siblings cast_sisca08 and d_sisca08 give the sector in the year of the row, while this column holds the final value on every year.
value_definition: A numeric sector code from the Standard Institutional Sector Classification of Australia as published in SESCA 2008 (Version 1.1). A value of 0 means unknown or missing.
limitation: Sector is not ownership, size or legal form. A foreign-controlled private company and a domestic one can share a code, and the type of legal organisation sits in cast_tolo rather than here. Because the column holds the latest value, a unit that was corporatised or privatised part way through the panel carries its post-change sector in every earlier year, which will misclassify exactly the transition a researcher wanted to study.
rationale: The SESCA 2008 (Version 1.1) release is the ABS publication that defines SISCA, its purpose and its categories, and it is the edition the column names. It also records that version 1.1 revised SISCA, which is why correspondences to the earlier SISCA are published alongside it.
evidence_quote: The Standard Institutional Sector Classification of Australia (SISCA) is a classification of institutional units which provides a framework for dividing the Australian economy into institutional sectors.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's label with the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so a reader learned neither what an institutional sector is nor that the 'latest' framing back-dates a sector change across the whole panel.

value_domain: Three-letter calendar month of business launch
value_source: ABS, BLADE Data and Legislation (Dealroom module)
variable_description: The calendar month Dealroom records as the month the business launched, repeated on every row for that ABN. Dealroom is a commercial private-market intelligence platform, so this is a curated third-party claim about the firm rather than an administrative event date, and it sits beside launch_year to give a month and year pair. The Dealroom module is a requestable BLADE addition covering 2025, so only ABNs Dealroom profiles carry any value at all.
value_definition: Three characters, initial capital, in English month abbreviation form: Jan, Feb and so on. Twelve valid values; missing where Dealroom holds a year but no month.
limitation: It is not the ABN registration date and not the ABS business birthdate, so a firm can trade for years before the month recorded here, or be recorded as launching before the entity that now holds the ABN existed. Because Dealroom profiles a self-selected slice of the startup and scaleup population, the absence of a launch month across most of BLADE says nothing about the businesses themselves.
rationale: The ABS page confirms Dealroom is a requestable BLADE module and gives its single reference year, which fixes the coverage; the meaning of the launch field is inferred from the custodian's wording and from what Dealroom publishes about itself.
evidence_quote: Dealroom: 2025
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's sentence about a time-invariant categorical month and the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, so nothing said whose claim the launch date is or how it differs from an ABN start date.

value_domain: Four-digit year of business launch
value_source: ABS, BLADE Data and Legislation (Dealroom module)
variable_description: The year Dealroom records as the year the business launched, held constant across every observation of the ABN. It is the coarser half of the launch date pair and is populated more often than launch_month, so firm age from Dealroom is usually only reliable to the year. Dealroom enters BLADE as a requestable module with a single reference year, 2025.
value_definition: A four-digit calendar year, stored as a number, for example 1990. The range is open at the early end because Dealroom records the launch of long-established firms as well as recent startups.
limitation: Firm age built from this column is not comparable with age built from Business Birthdate, which BLADE carries from 1992-93 on an administrative basis; the two can disagree by years for the same ABN after a restructure or an acquisition. A launch year also survives a change of owner, so it does not mark the start of the business as the ABN now measures it.
rationale: The ABS page establishes the module and its coverage year; the field's meaning follows from the custodian's wording and from Dealroom's role as a private-market data vendor.
evidence_quote: Dealroom: 2025
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's note that the variable is time-invariant, with the generic sentence printed twice, so a reader could not tell it apart from the administrative business birthdate already in BLADE.

value_domain: Lead content of an ore shipment, per cent
value_source: ABS, Australian Harmonized Export Commodity Classification (AHECC)
variable_description: The assayed lead content of an exported ore or concentrate shipment, expressed as a percentage of the shipment. It qualifies the export line rather than standing alone: multiplied by the shipment weight it gives lead content tonnes, which is how mineral exports are usually compared.
